topics.label: 19. Additional monitoring and the blue box

questions.q: Which annex of a centrally authorised product is the package leaflet?
questions.why: Annex I is the SmPC, Annex II the conditions, IIIA the labelling and IIIB the leaflet.

questions.q: Which QRD template version is current (October 2026)?
questions.why: Version 10.4 (February 2024); version 11 was consulted on in 2025 and is not yet in force.

questions.q: A section of the SmPC does not apply. What do you do?
options: Merge it with the next section
Keep the heading and write the template wording, such as "Not applicable."
questions.why: Headings are kept; the template gives the wording for sections that do not apply.

questions.q: What does text in angle brackets in the QRD template mean?
questions.why: Angle brackets mark alternatives; curly brackets mark information to fill in.

questions.q: Which document explains what goes in each SmPC section?
questions.why: The European Commission SmPC guideline, revision 2 (2009).

questions.q: What frequency is "common"?
questions.why: Very common ≥1/10; common ≥1/100 to <1/10; uncommon ≥1/1,000 to <1/100.

questions.q: Reactions known only from spontaneous reports usually go in which category?
questions.why: When the frequency cannot be estimated from the data, "not known" is used.

questions.q: Which word is not used for frequency in 4.8?
questions.why: Only the convention categories are used.

questions.q: What closes SmPC section 4.8?
options: The standard text on reporting suspected adverse reactions (Appendix V)
questions.why: The reporting statement points to the national systems in Appendix V.

questions.q: How are adverse reactions grouped in the 4.8 table?
options: By MedDRA system organ class and frequency
questions.why: System organ class first, then frequency within it.

questions.q: An oral tablet contains 0.6 mg sodium per tablet. What does the leaflet say?
options: The percentage of the daily intake
Not to take it on a low-salt diet
questions.why: Below 1 mmol (23 mg) per dose the "essentially sodium-free" statement applies.

questions.q: What is the threshold for the lactose statement in an oral product?
questions.why: Lactose has a zero threshold for oral products; a further statement applies at 5 g.

questions.q: Where in the leaflet do excipient statements go?
questions.why: Section 2 has a subheading for each excipient with a known effect.

questions.q: Why does aspartame need a statement?
options: It is a source of phenylalanine, harmful in phenylketonuria
questions.why: Aspartame (E 951) is a source of phenylalanine.

questions.q: Where does the outer carton name excipients with a known effect?
questions.why: Section 3 lists them, usually pointing to the leaflet.

questions.q: What does the inverted black triangle mean?
options: The medicine is under additional monitoring
It is for hospital use only
questions.why: It flags additional monitoring and invites reporting of suspected adverse reactions.

questions.q: Which medicine is automatically under additional monitoring?
options: One with a new active substance authorised after 1 January 2011
questions.why: New active substances (and biologicals) authorised after 2011 are included.

questions.q: What goes in the blue box?
options: National particulars a member state requires, such as price
questions.why: The blue box keeps national details separate from the common EU text.

questions.q: Where does the black triangle statement appear?
options: At the start of the SmPC and the leaflet
questions.why: Both the SmPC and the leaflet open with it.

questions.q: How long does additional monitoring usually last?
options: For the life of the product
questions.why: Typically five years from the reference date.

questions.q: What is the usual success standard for each user-test question?
options: At least 16 of 20 participants find and understand the information
questions.why: 90% find it and 90% of those understand it, about 81%, so 16 of 20.

questions.q: Who should not be a participant in a user test?
questions.why: Health professionals and people who know the medicine are excluded.

questions.q: How many participants are usually in each round?
questions.why: Rounds of 10, with revisions between them.

questions.q: What is bridging?
options: Showing a leaflet is similar enough to one already user tested
questions.why: A bridging report can replace a full test when content and layout are similar.

questions.q: Which is easier for patients?
options: "Tell your doctor straight away if you get leg pain or swelling"
"Manifestations of venous thromboembolism necessitate immediate consultation"
questions.why: Short, active sentences with everyday words.

questions.q: What must be in Braille on the packaging?
options: The name of the medicine (and the strength if there are several)
questions.why: Article 56a requires the name in Braille.

questions.q: What does the 2D data matrix on a prescription pack carry?
options: A QR link to a website
The unique identifier: product code, serial number, batch, expiry (and a national number where required)
questions.why: The unique identifier under Delegated Regulation 2016/161.

questions.q: What does section 18 of the labelling show?
options: The human-readable PC, SN and NN
questions.why: Section 18 is the human-readable form of the unique identifier.

questions.q: Since when have the safety features applied to most prescription medicines?
questions.why: Delegated Regulation 2016/161 applied from 9 February 2019.

questions.q: A company wants a QR code on the carton. What is needed?
options: Submission and assessment, with content consistent with the approved information
questions.why: EMA assesses QR codes and what they link to.

questions.q: Who reviews the translations of a centrally authorised product?
options: Member state linguistic experts, in the linguistic review
questions.why: Member states review the translations after the CHMP opinion.

questions.q: The English says 10 mg and the French says 25 mg. What kind of error is this?
options: A translation error that changes the meaning
questions.why: Numbers must be the same in every language.

questions.q: Why keep a term base?
options: To use approved terms consistently across documents and updates
questions.why: Consistent terms make review faster and avoid confusion.

questions.q: In French product information, which term is used for side effects?
questions.why: The QRD French template uses "effets indésirables".

questions.q: How many language versions does a centrally authorised product need?
options: Only the languages where it is marketed
All official EU languages plus Icelandic and Norwegian
questions.why: The decision covers the EU and the EEA states.

questions.q: Who decides the EU product information wording for a confirmed signal?
questions.why: PRAC recommendations include the wording and the deadline.

questions.q: Agreed PRAC wording implemented as it is: which variation?
questions.why: C.3.a covers implementation of agreed wording without new data.

questions.q: Where is the deadline for implementing a PRAC signal recommendation?
questions.why: Each recommendation sets its own deadline.

questions.q: What is a PSUSA?
options: A single assessment of periodic safety reports for an active substance
questions.why: PSUSA outcomes can change the product information of every product with the substance.

questions.q: In which languages does EMA publish PRAC signal wording?
options: English and all official EU languages
questions.why: Translations follow about three weeks after the meeting.

questions.q: What is the EU ePI standard based on?
questions.why: The EU ePI common standard uses HL7 FHIR.

questions.q: When did the EU ePI pilot run?
questions.why: Results were published in December 2024.

questions.q: Does this app produce FHIR ePI resources?
options: No, it shows a simplified structured view
questions.why: The ePI view is a teaching aid, not a FHIR export.

questions.q: What did the 2025 political agreement on new EU pharmaceutical legislation say about ePI?
options: Approved product information must be made available electronically (ePI)
questions.why: The agreement requires ePI; formal adoption and transition details follow.

questions.q: Is QRD version 11 in force?
options: No, it was consulted on in 2025
questions.why: The consultation closed in August 2025.

questions.q: What does Annex II, section B give?
options: The manufacturer of the active substance only
The legal status for supply, for example subject to medical prescription
questions.why: Section B sets the conditions or restrictions regarding supply and use.

questions.q: Which SmPC section gives the date of revision of the text?
questions.why: Section 9 is the date of first authorisation or renewal; section 10 the date of revision.

questions.q: What may a generic SmPC leave out under Article 11 of Directive 2001/83/EC?
options: Parts referring to indications or dosage forms still covered by patent law
questions.why: The rest of the SmPC follows the reference.

questions.q: Which particulars does a small vial label carry?
options: Name with route, method, EXP, Lot and contents
questions.why: Small immediate packaging carries the minimum particulars of Annex IIIA.

questions.q: What does "uncommon" mean in 4.8?
questions.why: The MedDRA frequency convention in the SmPC guideline.

questions.q: Within each frequency grouping, how are adverse reactions ordered?
questions.why: The guideline asks for decreasing seriousness within each frequency group.

questions.q: What is "very rare"?
questions.why: "Not known" is used when the frequency cannot be estimated.

questions.q: From what amount must an oral medicine state its sodium content?
options: 1 mmol (23 mg) per dose or more
questions.why: From 1 mmol per dose the leaflet gives the amount; below it, it may say essentially sodium-free.

questions.q: Below 1 mmol (23 mg) sodium per dose, what may the leaflet say?
questions.why: The annex gives that wording for small amounts.

questions.q: Who is the benzyl alcohol warning mainly about?
options: Babies and young children, who can have toxic reactions
questions.why: Benzyl alcohol can cause toxic and allergic reactions in infants and young children.

questions.q: Which legislation set up the list of medicines under additional monitoring?
questions.why: It amended Regulation 726/2004 (Article 23) to create the list.

questions.q: Who publishes the list of medicines under additional monitoring?
questions.why: EMA keeps and publishes the list.

questions.q: What is the blue box for?
options: National particulars on centrally authorised packs
questions.why: Article 57 lets member states require particulars such as price, shown in the blue box.

questions.q: Which guideline sets the EU readability requirements?
questions.why: It covers layout, wording and user testing.

questions.q: When can bridging replace a full user test?
options: When the leaflet is close in content and layout to one already tested
questions.why: Bridging relies on an earlier successful test of a similar leaflet.

questions.q: Which article says the leaflet reflects consultations with target patient groups?
questions.why: Article 59(3) of Directive 2001/83/EC is the basis for user testing.

questions.q: Which regulation sets the safety features?
questions.why: It sets the unique identifier and the anti-tampering device.

questions.q: What does the unique identifier contain?
options: Product code, serial number, batch and expiry (and a national number where required)
questions.why: These data are encoded in the 2D data matrix and printed in human-readable form.

questions.q: Which article requires the name in Braille?
questions.why: Article 56a of Directive 2001/83/EC.

questions.q: What does a term base hold?
options: The source term, the approved target term and notes
questions.why: It keeps terms consistent across documents and versions.

questions.q: A translation leaves out a sentence of section 2. What is it?
questions.why: Every sentence of the English must be translated.

questions.q: Who prepares the translations of a centrally authorised product?
questions.why: The company translates; member states review them.

questions.q: Which committee assesses safety signals in the EU?
questions.why: The Pharmacovigilance Risk Assessment Committee.

questions.q: Where does a holder find when PSURs are due?
questions.why: Annex II points to the list of Union reference dates.
questions.cite: QRD template, Annex II; Directive 2001/83/EC Article 107c(7)

questions.q: Which Annex II section gives the PSUR statement?
questions.why: Section C covers other conditions, including PSURs.

questions.q: What does ePI make possible that a PDF does not?
options: Searching and reusing structured sections across languages and versions
questions.why: Structure is the point of ePI.

questions.q: Does ePI change the approved content?
options: No: it is the same approved text in a structured form
questions.why: ePI carries the authorised product information.

questions.q: In this app's ePI view, what stays stable across versions?
questions.why: Stable identifiers let systems link to a section.
